questions.prompt: A team says, “Build us a recommender,” and immediately proposes item embeddings. What is the most important first response?

options.text: Choose the largest embedding model that fits the GPU budget
options.feedback: Model capacity is premature because the product surface, decision, and acceptable outcomes are still undefined.

options.text: Clarify the surface, user decision, candidate inventory, objective, and unacceptable outcomes
options.feedback: Correct. These constraints determine what is predicted, when it is predicted, and what the system must optimize or prevent.

options.text: Copy the architecture of a large video platform
options.feedback: A published architecture reflects another product's inventory, latency, and business constraints.

options.text: Start collecting clicks and decide the objective after launch
options.feedback: Unframed logging often omits exposures, positions, and guardrails that cannot be reconstructed later.

questions.explanation: A recommendation model is downstream of a product decision. Defining the surface and action makes the labels, latency budget, candidate set, metrics, and safety constraints concrete.
questions.followUp: How would your framing differ between a home feed, an email digest, and recommendations inside checkout?

questions.prompt: CTR rises 12%, but users hide more recommendations and seven-day retention falls. Which launch decision is most defensible?

options.text: Launch because CTR is the direct model objective
options.feedback: A proxy metric cannot override evidence that the product is creating longer-term harm.

options.text: Increase the click weight so the offline objective matches the CTR result
options.feedback: This strengthens the same proxy and can make the harmful behavior worse.

options.text: Hold the launch and evaluate qualified engagement with retention and negative-feedback guardrails
options.feedback: Correct. The decision should combine a useful primary outcome with explicit product-health constraints.

options.text: Ignore all online metrics until the model has accumulated one month of data
options.feedback: Waiting discards actionable guardrail evidence and exposes more users to a likely regression.

questions.explanation: Clicks are easy to optimize and easy to game. A production objective needs downstream value plus guardrails for dissatisfaction, concentration, safety, and long-term health.
questions.followUp: If retention is too slow for a canary decision, which faster proxy and guardrails would you trust?

questions.prompt: You have 50 million items and a 120 ms p99 deadline. Why is scoring every item with the final ranker the wrong design?

options.text: The final ranker cannot produce calibrated probabilities
options.feedback: Calibration is independent of whether the ranker evaluates fifty or fifty million candidates.

options.text: The network can never transfer item identifiers quickly enough
options.feedback: Identifier transfer matters, but model compute and feature retrieval dominate the infeasible exhaustive path.

options.text: Cost and latency grow with the full corpus, so retrieval must shrink the set before expensive scoring
options.feedback: Correct. A multi-stage funnel spends increasing compute on progressively smaller candidate sets.

options.text: Approximate retrieval is always more accurate than exact scoring
options.feedback: Approximation trades some recall for tractability; it is not inherently more accurate.

questions.explanation: The serving budget should be allocated across candidate generation, feature retrieval, pre-ranking, ranking, and slate constraints. Exhaustive final-model scoring does not scale with corpus size.
questions.followUp: How would you divide the latency budget if online feature reads become the dominant p99 stage?

questions.prompt: A new marketplace has sparse interaction history and must launch recommendations in three weeks. What should ship first?

options.text: A segmented popularity and freshness baseline with eligibility and diversity rules
options.feedback: Correct. It is observable, debuggable, cold-start friendly, and establishes a real benchmark quickly.

options.text: A transformer trained on the first week of clicks
options.feedback: Sparse, biased data and an unproven serving path make this a high-risk first release.

options.text: A per-user nearest-neighbor index rebuilt after every click
options.feedback: The operational complexity is not justified before there is enough user history or measured value.

options.text: Random recommendations to guarantee unbiased data
options.feedback: Full randomization damages relevance; bounded exploration can collect information without abandoning utility.

questions.explanation: A strong baseline creates product value, exposes logging gaps, and provides the control that later personalized models must beat.
questions.followUp: Which measured failure would justify moving from segmented popularity to personalization?

questions.prompt: The training table contains clicked items but not the items users saw and ignored. What is the most serious consequence?

options.text: The system cannot distinguish non-exposure from an observed negative outcome
options.feedback: Correct. Missing impression context corrupts negative sampling and makes evaluation selection-biased.

options.text: The model will necessarily overfit because every row is positive
options.feedback: Overfitting may occur, but the deeper issue is that the counterfactual candidate and exposure set is unknown.

options.text: The item embeddings will be too small
options.feedback: Embedding dimensionality does not recover missing exposure information.

options.text: Clicks can no longer be joined to user identifiers
options.feedback: Identity joins may still work; what is lost is what was eligible, ranked, displayed, and skipped.

questions.explanation: Every impression should preserve request context, candidates, positions, model and policy versions, and resulting actions. Click-only data cannot tell whether an item was rejected or never shown.
questions.followUp: Which fields must an impression event contain to support unbiased replay and position-aware evaluation?

questions.prompt: A ranking model looks excellent under a random interaction split but regresses in production. Which audit should happen first?

options.text: Increase the random test set from 10% to 20%
options.feedback: A larger random split preserves the same future-information leakage.

options.text: Check chronological splits and point-in-time feature joins
options.feedback: Correct. Future interactions or post-label aggregates can make offline ranking appear unrealistically strong.

options.text: Replace NDCG with accuracy
options.feedback: Accuracy ignores ranked position and does not correct temporal leakage.

options.text: Add production outcomes to the old training rows
options.feedback: That can introduce even more future information unless joined as of each historical decision time.

questions.explanation: Offline evaluation must recreate what the system knew at decision time. Chronological holdouts, point-in-time joins, and request-level candidate replay are core correctness requirements.
questions.followUp: How would you evaluate a new-item recommender when the item did not exist during most of the training window?

questions.prompt: The baseline is reliable, but returning users repeatedly see generic popular items despite rich histories. What is the next justified evolution?

options.text: Add personalized candidate retrieval and a learned ranker behind the existing fallback
options.feedback: Correct. The measured relevance gap now justifies personalization while preserving a safe baseline.

options.text: Remove popularity candidates entirely
options.feedback: Popularity remains useful for cold start, robustness, and coverage even after personalization is added.

options.text: Split every pipeline stage into a separate service
options.feedback: A relevance failure does not itself justify new network and operational boundaries.

options.text: Retrain the popularity list every minute
options.feedback: Fresher global popularity does not use the returning user's individual evidence.

questions.explanation: Architecture should evolve in response to a measured product limitation. Personalized retrieval expands relevant recall, and ranking learns interactions among user, item, and context signals.
questions.followUp: What evidence would tell you that retrieval recall, rather than ranking quality, is the current bottleneck?

questions.prompt: Collaborative retrieval performs well for established items but almost never surfaces new inventory. What is the best correction?

options.text: Increase the collaborative candidate quota
options.feedback: More candidates from the same source preserve its cold-item blind spot.

options.text: Union collaborative, content, freshness, popularity, and business-eligible sources with source quotas
options.feedback: Correct. Complementary sources cover different evidence and failure modes before ranking.

options.text: Force every new item directly into the final slate
options.feedback: Unbounded forced exposure can damage relevance and ignores eligibility and quality constraints.

options.text: Train only on interactions from new items
options.feedback: That sacrifices established-item performance and still does not create exposure for unseen inventory.

questions.explanation: Candidate generation is a portfolio problem. Multiple sources improve coverage and resilience; quotas and deduplication keep one source from crowding out the others.
questions.followUp: How would you measure the incremental recall contributed by each candidate source?

questions.prompt: Why is a two-tower model attractive for retrieving from tens of millions of items under a tight deadline?

options.text: It guarantees that the final ranking is globally optimal
options.feedback: Approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval does not guarantee the optimal final slate.

options.text: It can precompute item embeddings and compare one request embedding against an ANN index
options.feedback: Correct. Factorization moves most item computation offline and makes large-corpus retrieval tractable.

options.text: It eliminates the need for negative examples
options.feedback: Training still depends heavily on useful negatives and exposure-aware sampling.

options.text: It can use arbitrary cross-features between every user and item during retrieval
options.feedback: Independent towers limit direct cross-features; richer interactions are deferred to later ranking stages.

questions.explanation: Two-tower serving factorizes user/context and item computation. Item vectors are materialized and indexed, while the request tower produces the query vector online.
questions.followUp: Which useful interaction features are lost by factorization, and where would you reintroduce them?

questions.prompt: The final ranker meets quality goals on 100 candidates but violates latency when given 2,000. What should the pre-ranker optimize?

options.text: Perfect ordering of all 2,000 candidates
options.feedback: Perfect ordering duplicates the expensive ranker's job and defeats the latency purpose.

options.text: High recall of eventual winners while cheaply pruning obvious weak candidates
options.feedback: Correct. The pre-ranker protects final-ranker capacity without discarding strong candidates.

options.text: Maximum diversity regardless of relevance
options.feedback: Slate diversity is important, but aggressive early diversity can remove items the final stages need to compare.

options.text: The same feature set and model complexity as the final ranker
options.feedback: That would preserve most of the original cost rather than creating a cheaper stage.

questions.explanation: A pre-ranker is a recall-preserving filter. It should use inexpensive features and a simpler model to reduce candidate count before costly feature joins and scoring.
questions.followUp: How would you detect that the pre-ranker is silently capping the final ranker's achievable quality?

questions.prompt: You have strong tabular features, moderate data, CPU serving, and a 10 ms inference budget. Which first ranker is most defensible?

options.text: A gradient-boosted tree model with calibrated outputs
options.feedback: Correct. It is a strong, fast baseline for nonlinear tabular interactions and missing values.

options.text: The largest sequence transformer that fits in training memory
options.feedback: Training fit does not prove online latency, operational simplicity, or incremental product value.

options.text: A random forest with one tree per item
options.feedback: Per-item models create sparse data and an unmanageable serving and release surface.

options.text: No learned model because tabular features cannot support ranking
options.feedback: Tabular user, item, context, and historical features often support excellent initial rankers.

questions.explanation: Model choice follows data shape, latency, calibration, and operational constraints. A boosted-tree ranker is often the strongest honest baseline before sequence complexity is earned.
questions.followUp: What measured limitation would justify replacing the tree model with a sequence model?

questions.prompt: The top 20 independently scored results are all near-duplicate items from one creator. What layer should address this?

options.text: Increase every item's predicted click score
options.feedback: A uniform score change does not model interactions among selected items.

options.text: Apply a slate re-ranker with diversity, deduplication, and policy constraints
options.feedback: Correct. The utility of an item depends on what has already been placed in the slate.

options.text: Remove creator identity from all models and policies
options.feedback: Hiding the signal prevents concentration controls and can make the problem harder to observe.

options.text: Return only the single highest-scoring item
options.feedback: This avoids a duplicate slate by destroying the product requirement rather than solving it.

questions.explanation: Pointwise relevance is not slate utility. A final constrained re-ranker can trade a small amount of predicted relevance for coverage, freshness, safety, and user experience.
questions.followUp: How would you tune diversity without letting an arbitrary quota overwhelm relevance?

questions.prompt: Offline metrics are stable, but production scores shift after a feature pipeline rewrite. What is the strongest diagnostic?

options.text: Compare online feature snapshots with point-in-time offline values for the same requests
options.feedback: Correct. Request-level parity checks expose definition, freshness, default, and timestamp differences.

options.text: Retrain immediately on the shifted production scores
options.feedback: That can teach the model around a serving bug and erase the evidence needed to diagnose it.

options.text: Increase the model regularization parameter
options.feedback: Regularization does not reconcile two inconsistent feature computations.

options.text: Ignore the shift if overall request latency is unchanged
options.feedback: Serving correctness and system latency are independent dimensions.

questions.explanation: Training-serving skew is a data-contract failure. Shared definitions, timestamp semantics, freshness metadata, and parity sampling keep offline and online computation aligned.
questions.followUp: Which defaults should the model receive when one online feature group is stale rather than missing?

questions.prompt: A candidate model improves offline NDCG but changes score distribution sharply. What should happen before full rollout?

options.text: Promote automatically because the offline metric improved
options.feedback: Offline gain alone does not prove feature compatibility, calibration, latency, or product safety.

options.text: Replay and validate artifacts, shadow production traffic, then canary with guardrails and rollback
options.feedback: Correct. Each gate answers a different correctness or risk question before broader exposure.

options.text: Run the model only for users who previously clicked recommendations
options.feedback: That creates a selected cohort and does not validate the general serving path.

options.text: Deploy both models and average scores indefinitely
options.feedback: An unversioned permanent blend obscures ownership and does not replace a controlled release decision.

questions.explanation: A model release is a versioned software and data release. Artifact validation, replay, shadowing, canaries, and automated rollback protect against failures offline metrics cannot see.
questions.followUp: Which conditions should trigger automatic rollback during the first canary stage?

questions.prompt: Traffic is now global, and cross-region feature calls dominate tail latency. Which evolution best contains the problem?

options.text: Route every request to one central model region
options.feedback: Centralization preserves the cross-region latency and creates a larger failure domain.

options.text: Use regional serving cells with local online state and globally distributed versioned artifacts
options.feedback: Correct. Regional data paths bound latency and failure while a control plane coordinates safe versions.

options.text: Replicate every raw event synchronously to every region before responding
options.feedback: Global synchronous replication puts WAN availability and latency inside the request deadline.

options.text: Disable personalization outside the original region permanently
options.feedback: A temporary fallback can be safe, but it does not solve the justified global serving requirement.

questions.explanation: Global recommendation serving should keep the synchronous path local. Regional cells consume replicated events asynchronously and receive immutable model, feature, and policy versions.
questions.followUp: Which signals truly require global freshness, and which can tolerate eventual replication?

questions.prompt: One team owns a 200 RPS recommendation path whose stages scale together. Should it start as six networked services?

options.text: Yes, because ML systems require microservices
options.feedback: ML does not remove the latency, deployment, and failure costs of unnecessary service boundaries.

options.text: Yes, because every module should have its own database
options.feedback: Independent persistence without ownership or scaling needs creates consistency and operational debt.

options.text: No; keep clear in-process modules until ownership, scaling, runtime, or failure isolation diverges
options.feedback: Correct. A modular monolith preserves seams without paying distributed-systems costs prematurely.

options.text: No; all future versions must remain one unstructured file
options.feedback: A monolith can and should maintain strong module, contract, and test boundaries.

questions.explanation: Service boundaries should correspond to measurable independence. Until then, local calls simplify deadlines, transactions, debugging, and coordinated change.
questions.followUp: Which first component would you extract if candidate retrieval starts scaling independently?

questions.prompt: During a cloud migration, what is the safest way to choose managed services for this recommender?

options.text: Map each architectural responsibility and required guarantee to a managed capability
options.feedback: Correct. Responsibilities, latency, consistency, and failure behavior remain stable even when product names change.

options.text: Select the most recently announced service for each box
options.feedback: Recency does not establish workload fit or operational guarantees.

options.text: Use one database product for events, vectors, features, and analytics
options.feedback: Forcing unlike access patterns into one product can simplify a diagram while damaging the system.

options.text: Copy an AWS reference diagram and rename services for Google Cloud
options.feedback: Superficial naming ignores differences in semantics, regional behavior, and team experience.

questions.explanation: Cloud mapping comes after architecture. Define the needed queueing, stream, online-store, warehouse, ANN, serving, and observability properties, then choose services that satisfy them.
questions.followUp: Which components would you keep portable, and where is provider-specific integration worth accepting?

questions.prompt: A long-time user suddenly begins shopping for baby products. Why is relying only on their historical embedding risky?

options.text: Historical embeddings cannot be stored in an online feature store
options.feedback: They can be stored; the issue is that long-term history may lag current intent.

options.text: Session context and recent actions may be more predictive than the stable profile
options.feedback: Correct. A responsive system blends long-term preference with short-lived intent and contextual priors.

options.text: New intent should always replace all historical information
options.feedback: A single action may be noise; blending and decay are safer than unconditional replacement.

options.text: The user must be treated exactly like a brand-new account
options.feedback: Useful historical preferences still exist even when one intent dimension changes quickly.

questions.explanation: Cold start and intent shift require priors, content features, session evidence, freshness, and uncertainty-aware blending rather than one permanent user vector.
questions.followUp: How would you distinguish a durable preference change from a short-lived shopping mission?

questions.prompt: The model trains only on clicks from its own top-ranked results. What intervention best reduces the resulting feedback loop?

options.text: Log exposures and propensities, then use bounded randomized exploration
options.feedback: Correct. This creates information outside the current policy while preserving user utility.

options.text: Train for more epochs on the same click log
options.feedback: More optimization reinforces the same selected exposure distribution.

options.text: Remove all popular items from training
options.feedback: Popularity bias needs measurement and correction, not a blanket deletion that distorts reality.

options.text: Treat every unclicked catalog item as a negative
options.feedback: Most catalog items were never eligible or seen, so this manufactures false negatives.

questions.explanation: Recommendation changes what data is observed. Exposure-aware logs, stable holdouts, propensity information, and controlled exploration make policy effects measurable.
questions.followUp: How would you set an exploration budget for a high-stakes surface where poor recommendations are costly?

questions.prompt: The ANN service exceeds its deadline during a traffic spike. What should the request path do?

options.text: Retry until ANN returns so personalization is never lost
options.feedback: Retries can amplify the overload and consume the entire response deadline.

options.text: Fail the page because a non-personalized result is misleading
options.feedback: A bounded relevant fallback is usually better than losing the entire product surface.

options.text: Use a deadline-aware fallback such as cached, trending, or segmented-popularity candidates
options.feedback: Correct. Predefined degradation protects latency and availability while recording reduced quality.

options.text: Return the last raw ANN response even if it belongs to another user
options.feedback: Cross-user response reuse is both incorrect and potentially privacy violating.

questions.explanation: Fallbacks are part of the serving contract. Each dependency should have a timeout, stale-data policy, compatible default, and observable degradation path.
questions.followUp: Which fallback would you choose if ranking works but online user features are stale?

questions.prompt: CTR falls while model latency and error rate remain normal. Which investigation is most complete?

options.text: Inspect only aggregate prediction-score histograms
options.feedback: Scores can look stable while candidate coverage, feature freshness, or user slices regress.

options.text: Join data freshness, candidate-source coverage, feature distributions, model outputs, and product metrics by version and slice
options.feedback: Correct. Cross-layer evidence is needed to localize an ML product regression.

options.text: Rollback the API service without checking the active model or policy version
options.feedback: That may change nothing and can erase useful evidence about the real release.

options.text: Wait for the next training run to see whether CTR recovers
options.feedback: Retraining is not a substitute for diagnosing data, serving, policy, or product changes.

questions.explanation: ML observability spans inputs, retrieval, features, predictions, system health, decisions, and outcomes. Versions and slices connect those layers into a causal investigation.
questions.followUp: Which dashboards would help distinguish candidate-source loss from ranker drift within ten minutes?

questions.prompt: A new ranker increases watch time by repeatedly recommending sensational content from a small creator set. What should block launch?

options.text: Nothing, because watch time is the north-star metric
options.feedback: A single engagement proxy does not price safety, concentration, satisfaction, or ecosystem harm.

options.text: Only a statistically significant decrease in click-through rate
options.feedback: CTR does not capture the reported concentration and content-quality risks.

options.text: Predefined safety, negative-feedback, concentration, and creator-coverage guardrails
options.feedback: Correct. Product constraints make harmful optimization visible before full rollout.

options.text: The absence of a larger neural model
options.feedback: Model class does not determine whether the product objective and policy are safe.

questions.explanation: Recommendation systems allocate attention. Launch criteria must account for user welfare, policy, diversity, exposure concentration, and recovery paths alongside engagement.
questions.followUp: How would you measure creator concentration without guaranteeing equal exposure to low-quality inventory?

questions.prompt: A ranker release expects feature schema v8, but one serving cell still provides v7. What should prevent an unsafe score?

options.text: The model should infer missing field meanings from their names
options.feedback: Implicit inference is not a compatibility guarantee and can silently corrupt predictions.

options.text: A versioned request contract and artifact compatibility check before activation
options.feedback: Correct. The cell should reject or fall back before an incompatible bundle reaches traffic.

options.text: A retry against the same incompatible cell
options.feedback: Retrying does not change the schema mismatch.

options.text: A lower ranking threshold
options.feedback: Threshold changes cannot repair features with different definitions or shapes.

questions.explanation: The LLD should version feature schemas, model bundles, policy, candidate provenance, and response reasons. Compatibility tests make rollout failures deterministic rather than statistical surprises.
questions.followUp: Which fields would you include in a recommendation response to make a bad slate reproducible later?

questions.prompt: When should this recommendation architecture add another serving stage or service?

options.text: Whenever a well-known company publishes a more complex design
options.feedback: Another company's scale and constraints do not prove a bottleneck in this system.

options.text: At the start of every quarter to keep the architecture modern
options.feedback: Calendar-driven complexity has no connection to user or operational evidence.

options.text: When measured quality, latency, scale, ownership, or failure isolation limits justify the added boundary
options.feedback: Correct. Evolution should answer an observed failure with explicit success criteria.

options.text: Only after the existing system has suffered a total outage
options.feedback: Leading indicators and controlled experiments should trigger change before catastrophic failure.

questions.explanation: The system should evolve from baseline to personalized funnel to regional platform only when the current stage reaches a demonstrated limit. Every new component must earn its operational cost.
questions.followUp: What evidence would make you remove a stage rather than add another one?
